event.title: Howe, Manning & Almy: Boston’s First All-Woman Firm and the Changing Face of Architecture
event.description:
On view through May 27, 2027

 

This exhibit celebrates the first-known all-woman architecture firm in Boston, founded in 1900 by Lois Lilley Howe, one of the first women to study architecture at MIT, completing the 2 year Partial Course in Architecture in 1890. Howe, along with architects Eleanor Manning and Mary Almy, completed more than 900 commissions throughout the course of their company’s history. The exhibit will look at the role MIT’s architecture program played in supporting women in the field since the 1890s, as well as Howe, Manning & Almy’s influence on the built environment of Cambridge and the firm’s ecofriendly approaches to renovation.

 

The Maihaugen Gallery (14N-130) is open Monday through Thursday, 10am - 4pm, excluding Institute holidays.

event.title: Thesis Defense - Michael Law
event.description:
Speaker: Michael Law

Title: 

Symmetry, Stability, and Classification of Ricci Solitons

 

Abstract: 

 

Ricci solitons provide models for singularity formation and resolution in Ricci flow, while Ricci-flat asymptotically locally Euclidean (ALE) spaces arise as local models for the degeneration and desingularization of Einstein metrics. In this thesis, we develop a symmetry principle for steady and expanding gradient Ricci solitons and Ricci-flat ALE spaces under suitable asymptotic conditions. The principle relates symmetries at infinity to global isometries through dimension bounds on the kernel of the relevant Lichnerowicz operator. This kernel measures an obstruction to extending asymptotic symmetries and is closely connected to linear stability.

 

We apply this principle to characterize the Bryant solitons and the four-dimensional Appleton solitons under analytical hypotheses implied by strict stability. For the Appleton characterization, we also establish uniqueness within Appleton’s defining ansatz and strict stability of the four-dimensional examples. More generally, we classify four-dimensional steady gradient Ricci solitons with vanishing weighted Lichnerowicz kernel that are asymptotically cylindrical with link SU(2)/G, where G is a finite subgroup of SU(2), showing that they are quotients of Bryant or Appleton solitons. In the Ricci-flat ALE setting, bounds on the Lichnerowicz kernel yield characterizations of Eguchi–Hanson space and its higher-dimensional Calabi analogs.

 

Zoom Link: https://mit.zoom.us/j/92057992284

event.title: Boulez at 100
event.description:
As part of the worldwide celebration of Pierre Boulez’s centenary, acclaimed pianists Gloria Cheng and Ralph van Raat bring their touring program Boulez at 100 to MIT, hosted by MIT Media Lab Faculty Director Tod Machover. The program interweaves Boulez’s seminal piano works with music by John Cage, Morton Feldman, Frank Zappa, Magnus Lindberg, and Olivier Messiaen–composers who each echo, anticipate, or challenge Boulez’s vision across modernist, experimental, and boundary-crossing traditions.

Featuring chapters from Boulez’s rarely heard Structures Books I and II, the concert traces the rich artistic dialogue between Boulez and the composers whose music surrounds his own. Together, these works reveal Boulez not only as one of the twentieth century’s most influential composers, but also as an artist whose ideas have an increasing, surprising potential to resonate across generations, genres, and musical traditions.

event.title: Boulez at 100 Workshop
event.description:
Boulez at 100 Workshop
Tuesday, November 24, 2026 / 2:00-4:00pm
MIT Thomas Tull Concert Hall, Edward and Joyce Linde Music Building W18
201 Amherst St, Cambridge, MA

Following the Boulez at 100 performance, Tod Machover, Gloria Cheng, and Ralph van Raat come together for a public presentation exploring Pierre Boulez’s lasting influence on contemporary music, performance, and technology. 

Through conversation, musical examples, and excerpts from Machover’s Re-Structures—his homage to Boulez on his 90th birthday for two pianos and electronics—the presentation offers a deeper exploration of Boulez’s artistic legacy, enduring relevance, and passionate expression simmering beneath an intricately rational surface

Drawing on Cheng’s and Machover’s personal and professional relationships with Boulez, the presentation offers audiences a rare opportunity to explore his musical and institutional impact through the perspectives of artists who knew and worked closely with him.

event.description:
Join MIT's native and indigenous community to celebrate the Beaver Moon—so named because the full moon in November marks a time when beavers are in their prime condition, ready for winter. You are welcome to join the celebration:
 

4pm: Sacred Fire Ceremony and Storytelling with Sonya Atalay, Anishinaabe-Ojibwe; Leslie Jonas, Mashpee Wampanoag; and Jean-Luc Pierite, Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana. Sample cedar-tip tea and hear traditional stories, gathered around a sacred fire.


During normal dining hours: Enjoy a taste of Native American Heritage Month presented by MIT Campus Dining:

event.title: Number Theory Seminar
event.description:
Speaker: Murilo Corato Zanarella (Johns Hopkins)

Title: Relative Satake transforms and arithmetic level raising for unitary Friedberg--Jacquet periods

Abstract: 

For $F/F^+$ a CM extension, we consider the unitary Friedberg--Jacquet spherical pair $(H,G)=(U(r)\times U(r),U(2r))$ of totally definite unitary groups over $F^+.$ This talk concerns a "first explicit reciprocity law" in this situation, which is a certain congruence between automorphic periods of $(H,G)$ and cohomology classes obtained from special cycles in a Shimura variety related to a "nearby" spherical pair $(H^{(p)},G^{(p)})$. By the theory of bipartite Euler systems, this yields results towards the Beilison--Bloch--Kato conjecture for certain $H$-distinguished automorphic representations of $G$ at analytic rank $0$.

In this talk, I will discuss recent work which re-interprets such first reciprocity law in spectral terms. More precisely, I will explain how such congruences are encoded by a map between spherical functions on the spherical varieties $X^{(p)}=H^{(p)}\backslash G^{(p)}$ and $X=H\backslash G$, and how such map has a surprisingly simple spectral description via relative Satake transforms.
